# Condition decision fixtures

These files are the contract between two implementations of one small language.

A `when` in the definition — on a command, on a workflow, on a rollup's filters — is the same shape
everywhere: nested `all` / `any` over leaves of `{ field, operator, value }`. Cordango Platform
evaluates it in `Cordango.Semantics.ConditionEvaluator`. A standalone application generated by this
toolchain evaluates it with *different* code, in `Cordango.Standalone.Conditions.ConditionEvaluator`.

The duplication is deliberate, for the same reason the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) exist:
sharing the implementation would mean a change made for one product's reasons silently altering the
other's behaviour, and "silently" is the problem. A condition decides whether an approval is allowed
and whether a workflow fires. Nobody notices it answering wrongly until a month of records went the
wrong way.

So the rules are pinned here as **data**, and both implementations are asserted against the same data
by their own suites. Two implementations that must agree, and a test that fails the moment they stop.

## What these pin, and why each one is here

1. **`01` — comparison picks its rule from the operands.** A definition writes `value: 10000` as a
   JSON number and `stage: "lead"` as text; a record holds a decimal column and a text column. Both
   have to work without anybody declaring a type. Numbers compare as numbers even when one side is
   written as a string, because `9 > 10` is false and `"9" > "10"` is true.

2. **`02` — a blank is not comparable.** The rule every naive implementation gets wrong. Treating a
   missing number as zero makes `amount lt 100` true for every record nobody has filled in, and a
   workflow built on it fires on untouched rows. `lt` and `gt` are both false against a blank, which
   means they are not each other's negation — that is intended and it is worth knowing.

3. **`03` — the list operators, and the two boundary rules.** `between` is inclusive at both ends.
   `overlaps` depends on whether the endpoints carry a time: a bare DATE names a whole day, so a
   range ending Monday overlaps a window starting Monday, while anything with a time is half-open so
   a meeting ending at 10:00 does not collide with one starting at 10:00. That distinction is the
   entire point of a conflict check, and the front end applies the identical rule.

4. **`04` — composition and the value tokens.** `{{actor.id}}` makes one stored condition answer
   differently for two people. `{{today}}` and its day offsets come from the clock the caller passed,
   never from the machine, so a test can ask what a workflow would have done last March.

5. **`05` — nothing matches by accident.** Shapes that should never reach a running application,
   because the gate rejects them at author time. Pinned anyway: the safe reading of "I do not
   understand this guard" is that the guarded thing does not happen. A leaf naming neither a field
   nor a path is the sharp one — without a rule it would compare null against null and answer *true*.

## Format

```json
{
  "name": "what this file settles",
  "why": "why it is worth pinning",
  "now": "2026-03-15T10:00:00Z",     // the clock, for {{today}}
  "actorId": "person-001",           // who is asking, for {{actor.id}}
  "cases": [
    {
      "why": "optional, per case",
      "record":    { "stage": "lead" },
      "condition": { "field": "stage", "operator": "eq", "value": "lead" },
      "expect": true
    }
  ]
}
```

`record` is the record as JSON, exactly as the database holds it. `condition` is the definition's own
shape. `expect` is the answer both implementations must give.

## Adding one

Add a case whenever a condition surprises you, and write down in `why` what the surprise was. That
sentence is the actual deliverable — the assertion only stops the regression, while the sentence is
what stops somebody "fixing" the behaviour back.

Both suites pick up new files automatically:

- `dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` — the standalone implementation
- `dotnet test backend/AppBuilder.slnx` — the platform implementation

## One thing these do not pin

The generated application does not carry the JSON above. `ConditionEmitter` turns it into C# at build
time — `Condition.Leaf("stage", "eq", "lead")` — and the runtime evaluates *that*. So these fixtures
pin the two evaluators against each other, and the emitter's translation is pinned separately, by its
own tests and by compiling every generated application.
